 Hochul, Blakeman hit the campaign trail as early voting begins
 BY 
 Nái Rhoden
 Buffalo 
 PUBLISHED 6:00 AM ET Oct. 25, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 6:00 AM EDT Oct. 25, 2026 
 SHARE 
 BUFFALO, N.Y. — With just days until Election Day in New York, both Democratic incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul and her Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman’s campaigns are escalating their attacks over affordability and the governor's record.
 Hochul cast her ballot on Saturday and is rallying supporters in Buffalo, where she launched her political career.
 But as she seeks another four years in office, polling suggests trouble for the governor back home.
 Two independent polls show Bruce Blakeman leading upstate, while a Republican-commissioned survey puts him ahead 56% to 42% in the Buffalo region.
 Political analyst Jack O'Donnell says those numbers don't tell the whole story.
 "[The polls] have different makeups,” O'Donnell said. “In terms of the number of Republicans and Democrats. I still think Kathy Hochul is going to win Erie County."
 But when pressed about her standing back home, the governor turned to Blakeman's ties to President Donald Trump.
 "Republicans are running scared from Donald Trump,” Hochul said. “Everybody has enough sense to do that except Bruce Blakeman."
 Rallying in Staten Island, Blakeman turned the attention back to Hochul's record.
 "Our electric bills are 70% higher than the national average because of Kathy Hochul,” Blakeman said. “She has approved 48 utility rate hikes. Forty-eight. That's almost one a month. She's gotta go."
 And that criticism isn't coming from Blakeman alone.
 Following a GOP get-out-the-vote rally in Niagara Falls, Senate Minority Leader Rob Ortt echoed that argument.
 "New York state has gotten very unaffordable,” Ortt said. “Always been a high-priced state. It has gotten more unaffordable under Kathy Hochul's leadership in the last five years."
 But Hochul defended her record, continuing to point to the president's policies and their impact on Western New York businesses.
 "Whether it is the tariffs that have just crushed the economy of Western New York,” she said. “And I've done roundtables with businesses who say they don't know if they're going to survive."
 Blakeman is also proposing to eliminate state income taxes on the first $50,000 for single filers and $100,000 for joint filers.
 He says spending cuts would help pay for it, but questions remain about which programs would be affected.
 And with early voting now underway, New Yorkers are beginning to weigh in.
 Hochul also made campaign stops in Rochester and Syracuse Saturday, while Blakeman rallied supporters on Staten Island.
 Early voting continues through Nov. 1, ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3.
